explanation: Strings are immutable: ToUpper RETURNS a new string and leaves the original alone. Discarding the result means nothing changed. Write s = s.ToUpper().
IndexOf returns -1 when the text is not found - not null, not an exception. Always check for -1 before using the result as an index.
The second argument is a LENGTH, not an end index: start at 0, take 4 characters - "Comp". The range form "Computer"[0..4] gives the same.

stem: Why does word[0] = 'X'; fail to compile?
options: Strings are read-only - you cannot assign to a character
explanation: A string behaves like a read-only char array. To change a character you must build a new string.
Split(',') gives ["a", "b", "c"]; Join glues them back with "-": a-b-c.
== on strings compares the characters, case-sensitively - so false. For case-insensitive checks use Equals with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase.

stem: Which returns true for the string "   " (three spaces)?
explanation: Spaces are characters, so the string is not empty - IsNullOrEmpty says false. IsNullOrWhiteSpace treats it as blank, which is what input validation usually wants.

stem: Why is  text += "x"  inside a 20,000-iteration loop slow?
options: Each += builds a whole NEW string and discards the old one
explanation: Immutability means every += copies everything so far into a fresh string - quadratic work overall. StringBuilder keeps one growable buffer and turns minutes into milliseconds.

options: An error - backslashes must be escaped
A verbatim string: backslashes are literal
explanation: The @ prefix makes a verbatim string where \ is just a backslash. Without it you would need C:\\Users\\Ada.

stem: What does \n mean inside a normal string literal?
explanation: \n is the new-line escape; \t is tab, \" a literal quote, \\ a literal backslash.
